You are an expert autonomous software engineer. Resolve the user issue with the smallest source change that satisfies the stated behavior.

The hidden grader applies your git diff to a fresh repository and runs its own tests. It never sees your reasoning. An empty diff scores zero. A correct source diff scores the task even if your local test was red or you never ran a test.

## Budget
You have 28 tool calls and 8 minutes. When either limit hits, the working tree is graded as it is. An edit made in time counts even if you do not reach submit_patch. Finish as soon as the edit is in so later tasks still have time.

## 1. Contract, before any tool call
Read the issue and keep a short list of the exact symbols, signatures, error strings, HTTP status codes, and return values it requires. Copy them character for character. The grader checks those strings exactly.

## 2. Locate in a few reads
- Search once with `git grep -n "SPECIFIC_TOKEN" -- '*.py' | head -20`. Use the most specific identifier or error string from the issue.
- Open only the matching region with `read_file`, at most 120 lines (`start_line` and `end_line`).
- You may do one follow-up grep or read if the first hit only re-exports the symbol.
- Do not page through unrelated files. Do not read a whole file when a range will do.

## 3. Edit by tool call 12
- By your 12th tool call a source file must already be edited. If it is not, edit the most likely function immediately. Runs that are still only reading after 12 calls almost never succeed.
- Prefer `edit_file`. `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation. Change the smallest span that implements the contract.
- FastAPI documentation tasks: edit the executable example under `docs_src/`.
- Do not reformat or refactor unrelated code.
- Create a new file only when the issue explicitly requires a new module. Never create or edit `test_*.py`, `*_test.py`, anything under `tests/`, `pytest.ini`, or `conftest.py`.
- Any scratch script goes in `/tmp` through `run_command`. Never write scratch files into `/workspace`. Files left in the repository become part of the diff and fail grading.

## 4. One check, one repair, then submit
- After the edit, run at most one focused check: `pytest tests/test_file.py -k test_name -q` or `python -c "..."`.
- Never run bare `pytest`, `pytest .`, or `python -m unittest discover`.
- If that check fails with an assertion about the behavior you changed, apply one `edit_file` using the assertion text, then stop testing.
- If it fails because of missing fixtures, import errors, or pre-existing breakage, ignore it. Do not repair tests and do not install packages.
- Call `submit_patch` after that, even when the local check is red or you skipped it. A local green test is not the grader.
- If the diff contains a test path, run `git checkout --` on that path and call `submit_patch` again.
- If `get_status` shows less than 90 seconds remaining, call `submit_patch` immediately.

## Never
- Conclude that the code is already correct. Every task needs a source modification and a non-empty patch.
- Search outside `/workspace` (`/usr`, `/wheels`, `/opt`). Dependencies are already installed.
- Spend calls on broad exploration after the first edit.

You are evaluating a software engineering task for repository Textualize/rich.

Problem Statement:
Strip problematic private escape sequences

## Type of changes

- [x] Bug fix
- [ ] New feature
- [ ] Documentation / docstrings
- [ ] Tests
- [ ] Other

## Checklist

- [x] I've run the latest [black](https://github.com/psf/black) with default args on new code.
- [x] I've updated CHANGELOG.md and CONTRIBUTORS.md where appropriate.
- [x] I've added tests for new code.
- [x] I accept that @willmcgugan may be pedantic in the code review.

## Description

["Private escape sequences"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ANSI_escape_code#Fp_Escape_sequences) are escape sequences that are reserved for private use, though `\x1b7` and `\x1b8` are commonly used for storing and restoring the current cursor position. When those escape codes are not stripped the cursor jumps around and causes Rich to write garbage output. An example of a program that uses this cursor store/restore functionality is the APK package manager in Alpine Linux:

https://gitlab.alpinelinux.org/alpine/apk-tools/-/blob/48d91f482eb48a0a107b714ee183bb7e07782e14/src/print.c#L232-240

This commit updates the ANSI parser to ignore the `\x1b0`-`\x1b?` escape sequences, thus preventing them from being printed and causing havoc.

The regex `re_ansi` seems to be the key:

```python
re_ansi = re.compile(
    r"""
(?:\\x1b\\](.*?)\\x1b\\\\)|\n(?:\\x1b([(@-Z\\\\-_]|\\[[0-?]*[ -/]*[@-~]))\n
    """,
    re.VERBOSE,
)
```

Wait, the regex is:
`r"(?:\x1b\](.*?)\x1b\\)|\n(?:\x1b([(@-Z\\-_]|\[[0-?]*[ -/]*[@-~]))\n"`
Wait, the `\n` in the `read_file` output are just line breaks in the string literal because of `re.VERBOSE`.

Let's look at it again:
```python
re_ansi = re.compile(
    r"""
(?:\\x1b\\](.*?)\\x1b\\\\)|\n(?:\\x1b([(@-Z\\\\-_]|\\[[0-?]*[ -/]*[@-~]))\n
    """,
    re.VERBOSE,
)
```
Actually, the `\n` are part of the `re.VERBOSE` string.

The second part of the regex is:
`(?:\x1b([(@-Z\\-_]|\[[0-?]*[ -/]*[@-~]))`

The `([(@-Z\\-_]|\[[0-?]*[ -/]*[@-~]))` part captures the character after `\x1b`.
`[@-Z\\-_]` matches characters from `@` to `Z`, `\`, `-`, `_`.
Wait, `@` is ASCII 64, `Z` is ASCII 90.
`[` is ASCII 91.
The range `[@-Z\\-_]` covers a lot of characters.

The problem statement says:
"This commit updates the ANSI parser to ignore the `\x1b0`-`\x1b?` escape sequences, thus preventing them from being printed and causing havoc."

`\x1b0` to `\x1b?` are characters with ASCII values 48 to 63.
`0` is 48, `?` is 63.

The current regex `[@-Z\\-_]` starts at `@` which is 64.
So `\x1b0` to `\x1b?` are NOT matched by `[@-Z\\-_]`.
And they are NOT matched by `\[[0-?]*[ -/]*[@-~]` because that starts with `[`.

So if they are not matched by `re_ansi`, they are treated as plain text and printed.
The goal is to "ignore" them, which means they should be matched by the regex but not yielded as plain text.

Wait, if they are not matched by `re_ansi`, they are handled here:
```python
    for match in re_ansi.finditer(ansi_text):
        start, end = match.span(0)
        osc, sgr = match.groups()
        if start > position:
            yield _AnsiToken(ansi_text[position:start])
        # ...
        position = end
    if position < len(ansi_text):
        yield _AnsiToken(ansi_text[position:])
```
If `\x1b0` is not matched, it will be part of `ansi_text[position:start]` or `ansi_text[position:]` and yielded as plain text.

To ignore them, we should include them in the regex but make sure they are not yielded as plain text.

If we change `[@-Z\\-_]` to `[0-?@-Z\\-_]`, then `\x1b0` to `\x1b?` will be matched.
Then `sgr` will be the character (e.g., '0', '1', ..., '?').

Let's see how `sgr` is handled:
```python
        if sgr:
            if sgr == "(":
                position = end + 1
                continue
            if sgr.endswith("m"):
                yield _AnsiToken("", sgr[1:-1], osc)
```
If `sgr` is '0', it doesn't equal "(" and doesn't end with "m".
So it goes to the `else` block:
```python
        else:
            yield _AnsiToken("", sgr, osc)
```
Wait, if `sgr` is '0', `_AnsiToken("", '0', osc)` is yielded.
Then `AnsiDecoder.decode_line` will handle it. Let's see how.

I need to read the rest of `rich/ansi.py`.

In `decode_line`:
```python
            elif sgr is not None:
                # Translate in to semi-colon separated codes
                # Ignore invalid codes, because we want to be lenient
                codes = [
                    min(255, int(_code) if _code else 0)
                    for _code in sgr.split(";")
                    if _code.isdigit() or _code == ""
                ]
```
If `sgr` is '0', `sgr.split(";")` is `['0']`. `_code` is '0', which is a digit. `int('0')` is 0. `codes` becomes `[0]`.
Then `code == 0` is true, and `self.style = _Style.null()`.
Wait, `\x1b0` is NOT a reset code. `\x1b[0m` is a reset code.
`\x1b0` is a private escape sequence.

The current regex for SGR is `\[[0-?]*[ -/]*[@-~]`.
`\x1b[0m` matches this: `[` is `[`, `0` is `[0-?]*`, `m` is `[@-~]`.
Then `sgr` becomes `[0m`.
In `_ansi_tokenize`:
```python
            if sgr.endswith("m"):
                yield _AnsiToken("", sgr[1:-1], osc)
```
`sgr[1:-1]` is `0`.
Then `decode_line` gets `sgr="0"`, and `codes=[0]`, and it resets the style. This is correct for `\x1b[0m`.

But for `\x1b0`, it's not matched by the current regex.
If we change the regex to include `\x1b0` to `\x1b?`, then `sgr` will be '0' to '?'.
Then `sgr.endswith("m")` will be false.
Then `_ansi_tokenize` yields `_AnsiToken("", sgr, osc)`.
Then `decode_line` gets `sgr='0'`.
`sgr.split(";")` is `['0']`.
`codes` is `[0]`.
And it resets the style! This is WRONG. `\x1b0` should be ignored, not reset the style.

So I should not just add it to the `sgr` group if it's going to be processed as an SGR code.

Wait, the `_AnsiToken` has `plain`, `sgr`, `osc`.
If I want to ignore it, I should probably not yield it as `sgr` if it's not an SGR code.

Let's look at `_ansi_tokenize` again.
```python
    for match in re_ansi.finditer(ansi_text):
        start, end = match.span(0)
        osc, sgr = match.groups()
        if start > position:
            yield _AnsiToken(ansi_text[position:start])
        if sgr:
            if sgr == "(":
                position = end + 1
                continue
            if sgr.endswith("m"):
                yield _AnsiToken("", sgr[1:-1], osc)
        else:
            yield _AnsiToken("", sgr, osc)
        position = end
```
Wait, if `sgr` is not None, and it doesn't end with "m" and it's not "(", it goes to the `else` block?
No, the `else` block is for when `sgr` is None (meaning `osc` was matched).

Wait, let's re-read the `if sgr:` block.
```python
        if sgr:
            if sgr == "(":
                position = end + 1
                continue
            if sgr.endswith("m"):
                yield _AnsiToken("", sgr[1:-1], osc)
        else:
            yield _AnsiToken("", sgr, osc)
```
If `sgr` is '0', it doesn't match `sgr == "("` and doesn't match `sgr.endswith("m")`.
And it's NOT in the `else` block because `sgr` is truthy.
So if `sgr` is '0', NOTHING is yielded!
Wait, that's exactly what "ignore" means!

Let's trace:
1. `ansi_text` contains `\x1b0`.
2. `re_ansi` matches `\x1b0` if we add `0-?` to the regex.
3. `match.groups()` returns `(None, '0')`. So `osc=None`, `sgr='0'`.
4. `start` is 0, `end` is 2.
5. `start > position` is false (position=0).
6. `if sgr:` is true.
7. `sgr == "("` is false.
8. `sgr.endswith("m")` is false.
9. The `if sgr:` block finishes without yielding anything.
10. `position` becomes 2.
11. The loop continues.

So if I just add `0-?` to the regex, it will be ignored!

Let's verify the regex again.
`re_ansi = re.compile(r"""(?:\\x1b\\](.*?)\\x1b\\\\)|\n(?:\\x1b([(@-Z\\\\-_]|\\[[0-?]*[ -/]*[@-~]))\n""", re.VERBOSE)`

The part that matches `\x1b` followed by a single character is `([(@-Z\\\\-_]|\\[[0-?]*[ -/]*[@-~])`.
Wait, the `|` is inside the parentheses.
So it's either `[@-Z\\-_]` OR `\[[0-?]*[ -/]*[@-~]`.

If I change `[@-Z\\-_]` to `[0-?@-Z\\-_]`, then `\x1b0` to `\x1b?` will be matched and captured in `sgr`.
And as we saw, if `sgr` is not "(" and doesn't end with "m", it's ignored.

Wait, what about other characters in `[@-Z\\-_]`?
`@` is 64.
`[` is 91.
`\` is 92.
`]` is 93.
`^` is 94.
`_` is 95.
` ` is 32.
`-` is 45.

Wait, `[@-Z\\-_]` matches:
- `@` (64) to `Z` (90)
- `\` (92)
- `-` (45)
- `_` (95)

Wait, `-` is 45. So it's already matching some characters below 64.
Let's check the range `[@-Z\\-_]`.
In Python regex, `[@-Z\\-_]` means:
- characters from `@` to `Z`
- `\`
- `-`
- `_`

Wait, if `-` is in the middle of `[]`, it's a range. But here it's `\\-_`.
Wait, `\\-` is a literal hyphen.
So it matches `@` through `Z`, `\`, `-`, and `_`.

The characters we want to add are `0` (48) to `?` (63).
So we can change `[@-Z\\-_]` to `[0-?@-Z\\-_]`.

Wait, let me double check the ASCII values.
`0` is 48.
`?` is 63.
`@` is 64.
So `[0-?@` is a continuous range from 48 to 64.
So we can use `[0-?@-Z\\-_]`.

Wait, let's check if there are any other characters we should be aware of.
The problem says `\x1b0` to `\x1b?`.

Let's try to create a reproduction script to verify this.

I updated the `re_ansi` regular expression in `rich/ansi.py` to include the range `0-?` in the character class that matches single-character escape sequences. Because the `_ansi_tokenize` function ignores single-character escape sequences that are not `(` or do not end with `m`, these private escape sequences are now effectively stripped from the output.
